title: The Righteous and the Wicked
sum: After nine chapters of speeches, the book starts over with a new heading, "The proverbs of Solomon", and a new form: hundreds of two-line sayings, most of which stand alone. In chapters 10–15 the second line usually turns against the first with "but": the wise son and the foolish one, the hard worker and the lazy, the righteous and the wicked. Chapter 10 sets out the main pairs. It opens with a family (10:1), moves to money and work (10:2–5), and spends most of its time on the mouth: what the righteous say gives life, what the wicked say hides violence (10:6–21, 31–32).

The chapter's frame is God's rule over life. "The LORD will not leave the righteous to starve" (10:3), "It is the LORD's blessing that makes a person rich" (10:22), and "The fear of the LORD adds days" (10:27). Readers have always asked how sayings so confident fit a world where the righteous do suffer; the notes at 10:27 and 12:21 take that up.
readings: Read one saying at a time

Most of these sayings were made to be remembered alone, like any proverb, and applied when the moment came. Read this way, each verse is a small, complete lesson, and two sayings that pull in different directions (10:15 and 18:11) are tools for different situations.

Many recent scholars (Knut Heim, Bruce Waltke) find small groups linked by sound, key words and themes: 10:1–5 on family and work, 10:18–21 on speech, 10:27–30 on the future of the righteous. Read this way, neighboring sayings comment on each other.

views.H: The heading ties the collection to Solomon, whose "three thousand proverbs" are recalled in 1 Kings 4:32. The sayings assume farms, harvests, households with servants, a town gate and a king, the world of Judah under its kings. Nothing in chapter 10 requires a date; the sayings could be older than the book and older than Solomon.
views.C: Critical scholars see 10:1–22:16 as one of the oldest parts of the book, perhaps made of smaller collections joined by editors (10–15 and 16:1–22:16 differ in style). The 375 sayings, the number of Solomon's name, suggest a careful editor. Repeated half-lines (10:6b and 10:11b; 10:8b and 10:10b) show the collectors drew on a store of stock lines.
views.W: Egyptian teachers prized good speech as a treasure (Ptahhotep) and set the "silent man" against the "heated man" (Amenemope); Proverbs 10 shares that outlook on the mouth. Its contrast of the righteous and the wicked is also found in Egyptian wisdom, but the steady link to "the LORD" is Israel's own.
views.J: The rabbis drew sayings from this chapter into Jewish life. "The righteous are remembered with blessing" (10:7) became the formula said after the name of the dead; "righteousness rescues from death" (10:2) was read as a promise to those who give charity; and "the righteous man is a foundation" (10:25) as the righteous one on whom the world stands (Bavli Chagigah 12b).
views.X: The New Testament quotes 10:12 twice (1 Peter 4:8; James 5:20): love covers a crowd of sins. Jesus' parable of the two builders (Matthew 7:24–27) echoes 10:25. The church fathers read the chapter as moral teaching for Christian households, and Protestant readers prized it as everyday wisdom under God's providence.

deep.b:
Almost every verse in chapters 10–15 has two lines, and the second line usually contrasts with the first. Scholars call this antithetic parallelism. The contrast does more than repeat: it fills in what each line leaves out. In 10:1 the father is glad and the mother grieves, but the point is that a son's character affects both parents. In 10:4 slack hands make a person poor and diligent hands bring riches, and together the lines say that work, not luck, usually decides a household's food. The Plain English Translation keeps the two lines and the "but" wherever the Hebrew has them, and keeps each line short, as the Hebrew does (most lines have three or four Hebrew words).

Words that sound alike also tie the lines together, and some can be heard in English: "fake pay" and "real pay" in 11:18, "in comes arrogance, and in comes shame" in 11:2. Others are explained in the notes.

Chapter 10 names the righteous (tsaddiq) thirteen times and the wicked (rasha') twelve times. These are not two social classes. The righteous are people who live rightly with God and neighbor; the wicked are those who do not. The sayings promise that the two roads end in different places: blessing, memory and life for the one, and a rotting name, ruin and a short life for the other (10:6–7, 16, 24–25, 27–30). Proverbs states this as the way God's world works. Job and Ecclesiastes test it against cases that do not fit, and the Bible keeps all three books side by side.

For these chapters the writer checked the following witnesses directly: the Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text, AD 1008) with its marginal readings, the Ketiv and Qere, as given in the STEPBible edition; and the Old Greek in Codex Vaticanus as printed in Swete's edition, with Swete's notes on the readings of Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus. The Greek is quoted from Vaticanus, which is also the main base of Rahlfs' edition of Proverbs; readings found only in Vaticanus, Sinaiticus or Alexandrinus are named by codex. The Dead Sea Scroll 4QProv-b, the Syriac Peshitta, the Targum and Jerome's Latin are cited only as reported by their editors and by the commentaries named in the notes.

echoes: 1 Kings 4:32; 15:20; 17:9; 18:10–11; 1 Peter 4:8; James 5:20; Matthew 7:24–27; Psalm 37:9–11; Psalm 112:6; Psalm 127:1–2; Job 21:7; Ecclesiastes 7:15

settings.what: The first Solomon collection opens: sayings on the righteous and the wicked, work and speech
settings.by: the sages who gathered "the proverbs of Solomon" (10:1), speaking in short, anonymous sayings
settings.to: young men of Israel's households, and perhaps young scribes and officials in training; the son of 10:1 is the son of any family
settings.when: collected under the kings of Judah, many scholars think, from sayings that may be older; the book's heading links them to Solomon (1 Kings 4:32)
settings.why: To give a young person a stock of short, memorable rules for a whole life: how to work, how to speak, how to treat parents and neighbors, and what each road leads to under the LORD's rule. Knowing that these were teaching sayings for the young explains their confident, black-and-white style: they are meant to form habits, not to cover every case.
settings.readers: The finished book's readers, Jews of the Persian and Greek periods and later the church, read these sayings after the long speeches of chapters 1–9, so they heard every "wise son" as the son who had listened to his father and to Wisdom.
views: Many scholars (for example McKane and Fox) think sayings like these were collected and used to train young scribes and officials at the court in Jerusalem, as Egyptian instructions were used in Egypt; 25:1 shows royal scribes at work on Proverbs.
Others (for example Claus Westermann) think most of the two-line sayings began as folk wisdom among farmers and households and were only later written down by scribes.
Most critical scholars think the collection reached its final form, with chapters 1–9 in front of it, in the Persian period, when the book became a textbook for Jewish life.

title: Honest Scales and a Generous Hand
sum: Chapter 11 opens in the marketplace: "Scales that cheat are abhorrent to the LORD" (11:1). From there it moves through pride and integrity (11:2–8), to the town that rises or falls with its people's words (11:9–14), to money matters: guaranteeing a stranger's loan (11:15), the ruthless and the cruel (11:16–17), and a run of sayings on generosity and hoarding (11:24–28). "Someone scatters freely, and he ends up with still more" (11:24) is a paradox the New Testament takes up (2 Corinthians 9:6).

The chapter ends with two of the book's best-known lines. "The fruit of a righteous man is a tree of life" (11:30) brings back the tree of Eden, and its second half, in the KJV "he that winneth souls is wise", became a motto for evangelism, though the Hebrew is hard. The last verse (11:31) is quoted in 1 Peter 4:18 in its Greek form: "If the righteous person is barely saved, where will the ungodly man and the sinner appear?"

views.H: The sayings fit a town economy of farmers, traders and lenders: silver weighed on scales, loans sealed with a handshake, grain stored against hard years. Archaeologists have found many inscribed stone weights from Judah of the 700s–600s BC, the world these sayings assume.
views.C: The chapter shows the collectors grouping sayings by theme and catchword: "town" in 11:10–11, "neighbor" in 11:9 and 11:12, and "generous" and "blessing" in 11:24–26. The Greek translation adds lines (11:16) and drops others (11:4), signs of a freer translation of Proverbs than of most books.
views.W: Amenemope's chapter 16 forbids moving the scales or altering weights, as 11:1 does, and Egyptian and Mesopotamian law codes protected honest measures.
views.J: The rabbis built on 11:13 their teaching against lashon hara, harmful talk, and read 11:4 with 10:2 as a promise to those who give charity. "The fruit of a righteous man is a tree of life" was heard with 3:18, "To those who grab hold of her she is a tree of life", which the synagogue sings of the Torah as the scroll is returned to the ark (Etz chayyim hi).
views.X: Christians have read 11:24–25 as the logic of generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:6–9), 11:30 as a call to evangelism (Spurgeon's The Soul Winner), and 11:31 through 1 Peter 4:18 as a word about the coming judgment that begins with God's household.

deep.b:
The Hebrew of 11:31 argues from lesser to greater: if the righteous are repaid on earth, then surely the wicked and the sinner are. "Repaid" (yeshullam) covers both reward and punishment, and many Jewish interpreters took it as the punishment the righteous receive for their few sins in this life. The Old Greek reads, "If the righteous is barely saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear?" (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete). The translator seems to have read yeshullam in the sense of being made whole or saved, and turned the statement into a question about the judgment.

1 Peter quotes that Greek word for word. Writing to churches in Asia Minor under pressure, Peter says that "the time has come for judgment to start from God's house" (1 Peter 4:17) and then cites Proverbs: "If the righteous person is barely saved, where will the ungodly man and the sinner appear?" (1 Peter 4:18). He does not mean that salvation is uncertain; he means that God's people pass through suffering on the way, so the outlook for those who reject God is far worse. The Hebrew and the Greek share the argument from lesser to greater; Peter's use shows how the early church read the Old Testament in Greek.

Chapter 11 has more sayings about money than any other in these chapters, and they do not say that wealth is good or bad in itself. They condemn cheating (11:1), warn against trusting in riches (11:4, 28) and against careless guarantees (11:15), set the ruthless beside the gracious (11:16), and praise the generous (11:24–26). The one who sells grain in a famine is blessed (11:26): fair dealing, not only charity, serves the poor. The note at 10:15 explains how Proverbs observes the power of wealth without approving it.

echoes: Deuteronomy 25:13–16; Leviticus 19:35–36; Amos 8:4–6; Genesis 42:6; Esther 7:9–10; 2 Corinthians 9:6–9; Psalm 112:9; Genesis 2:9; Revelation 22:2; 1 Peter 4:17–18

settings.what: Sayings on honest trade, the town, money and generosity
settings.by: the sages of the first Solomon collection
settings.to: young men who would soon trade, lend, inherit land and take part in the life of the town gate
settings.when: in the same collection as chapter 10; the economic sayings fit Judah's towns under the monarchy
settings.why: To teach that honesty in business is a matter of the LORD's own favor (11:1), that a town's welfare rides on the character and speech of its people (11:10–11), and that generosity is wiser than hoarding (11:24–26). For a young man about to handle money and contracts, the sayings gave rules of thumb with God behind them.
settings.readers: Jewish readers after the exile, many of them small farmers and traders under foreign rule, heard these sayings as the ethics of the covenant community; Nehemiah 5 shows how pressing debt and hoarding were in that age.
views: Many scholars (for example McKane and Fox) think sayings like these were collected and used to train young scribes and officials at the court in Jerusalem, as Egyptian instructions were used in Egypt; 25:1 shows royal scribes at work on Proverbs.
Others (for example Claus Westermann) think most of the two-line sayings began as folk wisdom among farmers and households and were only later written down by scribes.

title: Lips That Wound and Heal
sum: Chapter 12 begins with a blunt line, "To love discipline is to love knowledge; one who hates being rebuked is as dumb as an animal" (12:1), and goes on to the household: the woman of strength who is her husband's crown (12:4), the righteous man who cares for his animals (12:10), the farmer who works his land (12:11). Its center is a long run of sayings on speech (12:13–23): the honest witness and the liar, the words that stab like a sword and the tongue of the wise that heals (12:18), the lip that tells the truth and the lie that lasts "only for a wink" (12:19).

The chapter ends with work (12:24, 27) and with one of the hardest lines in the book: "On the road of righteousness there is life; and where its path goes, death is not" (12:28). Whether the sages here glimpsed a life beyond death is still debated.

views.H: The sayings on witnesses (12:17, 19) assume Israel's courts at the town gate, where a lying witness could cost a life. "Forced labor" (12:24) recalls the labor gangs of Solomon and later kings (1 Kings 5:13; 1 Kings 12:18).
views.C: Several verses here are among the hardest in Proverbs (12:12, 26, 27, 28), and the Greek often reads differently. Scholars propose many corrections; the Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and gives the alternatives in notes and variants.
views.W: Egyptian instructions teach the same restraint in speech and the same respect for the honest witness. The "woman of strength" has no close Egyptian parallel in the instructions, which seldom praise wives so highly.
views.J: Jewish law draws from texts like 12:10 the principle of avoiding the suffering of animals (tsa'ar ba'alei chayyim).
views.X: Christian readers have linked the sayings on the tongue with James 3 and Jesus' words about the fruit of the mouth (Matthew 12:33–37), and many, with Psalm 16 and John 8:51, have read 12:28 as a promise of eternal life.

deep.h: The woman of strength and the women of Proverbs 10–15
deep.b: Proverbs was first spoken to young men, and its sayings about women look at them from that side: a wife who is her husband's crown or rot in his bones (12:4), a beautiful woman without sense (11:22), a gracious woman who wins honor (11:16), the wisest of women who builds her house, while folly tears it down (14:1). Modern readers notice that there are no matching sayings about husbands. They also notice how much power the sayings give women: the household's honor, health and future lie in her hands. The phrase "woman of strength" ('eshet chayil) returns at 31:10, where a whole poem describes her running a household, trading and caring for the poor, and in Ruth 3:11, where Boaz says the whole town knows Ruth is "a woman of worth".

echoes: Psalm 73:22; 31:10; Ruth 3:11; Deuteronomy 25:4; Exodus 20:16; Deuteronomy 19:15–19; James 3:5–8; Matthew 12:33–37; 1 Kings 5:13; Psalm 16:10–11

settings.what: Sayings on correction, the household, honest witness and the power of words
settings.by: the sages of the first Solomon collection
settings.to: young men about to marry, farm, testify in court and take their place among the town's adults
settings.when: in the same collection; the sayings assume a farming household with servants and animals and a town court
settings.why: To make a young man value correction (12:1, 15), choose a wife of strength (12:4), work his land (12:11, 24, 27) and above all guard his tongue (12:13–23), because in a small town a word in court or at the gate could save or ruin a life. Knowing the audience explains why speech gets so much space: these were the habits that made a trustworthy man.
settings.readers: For the book's later readers, Jews and then Christians who no longer lived in Judah's villages, these sayings became general wisdom about honesty, marriage and the tongue.
views: Many scholars (for example McKane and Fox) think sayings like these were collected and used to train young scribes and officials at the court in Jerusalem, as Egyptian instructions were used in Egypt; 25:1 shows royal scribes at work on Proverbs.
Others (for example Claus Westermann) think most of the two-line sayings began as folk wisdom among farmers and households and were only later written down by scribes.

title: The Father's Discipline
sum: Chapter 13 opens and closes with the family. "A father's discipline: a wise son takes it in" (13:1), and near the end comes the most debated saying in these chapters: "Whoever keeps back his rod hates his son, but one who loves him seeks him out early with discipline" (13:24). Between them are sayings on guarding the mouth (13:2–3), on rich and poor (13:7–8, 11, 22–23), on hope delayed and longing fulfilled (13:12, 19), and on choosing companions: "The one who walks with the wise grows wise" (13:20).

The rod saying has been used for centuries to defend beating children, and in recent decades it has been debated by Jews and Christians alike. The deep dive below sets out what the Hebrew says, how the saying was used and how it is read today, without softening the text. The chapter also contains the first of the verses preserved in the Dead Sea Scroll 4QProv-b.

views.H: The sayings assume a patriarchal household in which the father teaches and corrects his sons, and in which physical punishment was ordinary, as it was everywhere in the ancient world. 13:22's inheritance "to grandchildren" reflects Israel's ideal of family land kept for good.
views.C: The repeated words "does not hear a scolding" in 13:1 and 13:8 show the collectors placing sayings with a shared phrase near each other. The Greek adds couplets after 13:9 and 13:13 and lacks 13:6 in Codices Vaticanus and Sinaiticus (Alexandrinus has it, and Rahlfs prints it).
views.W: Egypt's scribal schools and the Aramaic sayings of Ahiqar took the rod for granted in training boys; Proverbs shares that world. Ptahhotep ends with praise of the son who listens to his father, the theme of 13:1.
views.J: The midrash on Exodus opens with 13:24, reading the stories of Ishmael and Absalom as warnings against fathers who would not correct their sons (Exodus Rabbah 1:1). The Talmud sets limits on striking children, and modern Israeli law forbids corporal punishment by parents.
views.X: Hebrews 12:5–11 applies the logic of discipline to God's training of his children, quoting 3:11–12. Many Christian parents and teachers through history used 13:24 to justify physical punishment; today Christians are divided, some defending moderate spanking and others urging non-physical discipline (Ephesians 6:4).

deep.h: The rod in Proverbs 13:24: what it says, how it was used, how it is read
deep.b:
What the Hebrew says. Chosekh shivto sone' veno: "one who holds back his rod hates his son". The shevet is a real stick, the same word used for beating fools (10:13; 26:3) and for the shepherd's club of Psalm 23:4. The saying means physical punishment, and the Plain English Translation keeps "rod". Its second line, ve'ohavo shicharo musar, "but one who loves him seeks him (early) with discipline", uses musar, the book's broad word for teaching and correction (see the note at 1:2). The point of the verse is love: a parent who never corrects a child is acting as if he hated him. "Spare the rod and spoil the child" is not a Bible verse; it is best known in this form from Samuel Butler's poem Hudibras (1664), though the proverb is older (it is already in Langland's Piers Plowman, late 1300s).

How it was used. In the ancient world, beating was a normal part of schooling, in Egypt and in the Aramaic sayings of Ahiqar as in Israel (compare 22:15; 23:13–14; 29:15). The rabbis read 13:24 as a warning to soft fathers (Exodus Rabbah 1:1) but also limited the practice: a teacher should strike a child only with a light strap (Bavli Bava Batra 21a), and a father who strikes a grown son is condemned for putting a stumbling block before the blind (Bavli Moed Katan 17a). In the church, Augustine remembered the beatings of his school days with pain (Confessions, book 1), and many Christian educators, Wesley among them, taught that a child's will must be broken early. For centuries the verse was quoted in homes and schools to justify physical punishment.

How it is read today. Modern Jewish and Christian readers agree that the verse calls for loving, active discipline and condemns neglect. They differ over the rod. Some evangelical teachers, notably James Dobson, defend moderate spanking as biblical; others, such as William Webb, argue that Scripture's own direction (Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:21) moves beyond physical punishment while keeping the call to correct. Israel's Supreme Court banned corporal punishment by parents in 2000, and many churches and child-welfare bodies now urge non-physical discipline. Because the disagreement runs through traditions rather than between them, this page does not set it out as a contest between churches.

Two small Dead Sea Scrolls contain parts of Proverbs. One of them, 4QProv-b (also numbered 4Q103), preserves fragments of chapters 13, 14 and 15. As reported by Eugene Ulrich and his co-editors in Discoveries in the Judaean Desert 16, and in Abegg, Flint and Ulrich's The Dead Sea Scrolls Bible, the surviving text is close to the Masoretic Text, with mostly small differences of spelling. It is a witness that the Hebrew of these chapters was already much as we have it before the time of Jesus, while the Greek translation, with its additions and different order, went its own way.

deep.title: Claude's theory: "does not hear a scolding" as a hinge
deep.b: The four Hebrew words of 13:1b return as 13:8b with a new sense: the mocker will not listen to a scolding, and the poor man never hears a threat. I suggest the repetition is a deliberate hinge that ties the opening family saying to the money sayings of 13:7–11, and invites the reader to compare two kinds of deafness: the fool's, which ruins him, and the poor man's, which protects him. This overlaps with Knut Heim's work on clusters and catchwords in 10:1–22:16, which finds many such links; the specific reading of 13:1 and 13:8 as a pair is my own.

echoes: 3:11–12; 22:15; 23:13–14; 29:15; Hebrews 12:5–11; Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:21; Deuteronomy 8:5; 2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 23:4; 1 Corinthians 15:33; 2 Corinthians 6:10; Job 27:16–17

settings.what: Sayings on a father's discipline, the mouth, wealth and companions
settings.by: the sages of the first Solomon collection; the voice of a father is in the background of 13:1 and 13:24
settings.to: sons in a household, and the fathers responsible for them; 13:24 speaks to the parent
settings.when: in the same collection; the sayings assume a household where the father taught and corrected his sons
settings.why: To persuade the son that correction is good for him (13:1, 18) and the father that correcting is an act of love (13:24), and to warn both about easy wealth and bad company (13:11, 20). Knowing that 13:24 was addressed to a father in a world where beating was normal explains its tone; it is an argument against neglect.
settings.readers: For the book's later readers in Jewish and Christian homes, the chapter became a parenting text, and 13:24 one of the most quoted verses about raising children.
views: Many scholars (for example McKane and Fox) think sayings like these were collected and used to train young scribes and officials at the court in Jerusalem, as Egyptian instructions were used in Egypt; 25:1 shows royal scribes at work on Proverbs.
Others (for example Claus Westermann) think most of the two-line sayings began as folk wisdom among farmers and households and were only later written down by scribes.

title: The Wisest of Women
sum: Chapter 14 opens with a picture: "The wisest of women builds her house, but folly tears it down with her own hands" (14:1). The line recalls Wisdom's house of 9:1, and many scholars re-point the Hebrew to read "Wisdom" here (see the variants). The sayings that follow set the shrewd against the naive (14:15–18), the honest witness against the liar (14:5, 25), and the patient against the hothead (14:17, 29). Some look inward: "Only the heart knows how bitter it feels" (14:10), and "A heart may hurt even while it laughs" (14:13). One warns about self-deception: "There is a road that looks straight to a person, but in the end it comes out on the roads of death" (14:12; repeated at 16:25).

The chapter also turns to the poor and the nation. Oppressing the poor is "taunting the one who made them" (14:31), and the last verses speak of king and people: "Righteousness raises a nation up, but sin brings peoples shame" (14:34).

views.H: The closing sayings (14:28, 35) speak of a king, his people and his servants, the world of a royal court. 14:4's oxen and feed trough belong to the farm. The two settings sit side by side in the collection.
views.C: 14:12 and 16:25 are the same saying, kept twice; the collection has many such doublets, which suggests it was made from smaller collections. The Greek differs at several points (14:17, 24, 32, 33), and some of its readings may be older than the Hebrew.
views.W: The contrast between the hot-tempered and the patient man (14:17, 29) is a favorite theme of the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope. The protection of the poor as a duty to God is found in Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts too, but Proverbs grounds it in God as the poor man's Maker (14:31).
views.J: The rabbis made 14:28, "The more people there are, the more splendid the king", a rule for praying and blessing together (Bavli Berakhot 53a), and read 14:34 as a saying about the charity of the nations (Bavli Bava Batra 10b).
views.X: Christians link 14:31 with Matthew 25:31–46 and James 2. 14:12 has often been preached as a warning that sincerity does not make a road right. "Righteousness exalteth a nation" (14:34, KJV) is often quoted in public life.

deep.b: Kings appear only at the end of chapter 14 in these chapters (14:28, 35), then far more often in 16:10–15 and later. The sayings take for granted that a king's glory lies in his people and that his favor and anger shape a servant's career. Scholars who think the collection was used in a court school point to sayings like these; others note that every Israelite lived under a king and needed to know how to behave before one. Either way, the king is not above the sages' standards: he too needs a large and thriving people, and he too must reward sense and punish disgrace.

settings.what: Sayings on wisdom and folly, the shrewd and the naive, truth and lies
settings.by: the sages of the first Solomon collection
settings.to: young people, especially "the naive" (14:15, 18) who are easily led, and the households they belonged to
settings.why: To teach the naive to be shrewd: to test what they hear (14:15), keep away from fools (14:7), control their temper (14:17, 29) and trust the fear of the LORD as a refuge (14:26–27). Knowing the audience was young and impressionable explains the stress on watching one's step.
settings.readers: The book's later readers heard 14:1 beside 9:1 and read the whole chapter as Wisdom's household rules.
views: Many scholars (for example McKane and Fox) think sayings like these were collected and used to train young scribes and officials at the court in Jerusalem, as Egyptian instructions were used in Egypt; 25:1 shows royal scribes at work on Proverbs.
Others (for example Claus Westermann) think most of the two-line sayings began as folk wisdom among farmers and households and were only later written down by scribes.

settings.what: Sayings on king, nation and the poor
settings.by: the sages of the first Solomon collection
settings.to: those who served or might serve at court, and the king himself (14:28, 35)
settings.when: in the same collection; the sayings assume Judah's monarchy
settings.why: To remind officials and rulers that a king's glory is his people (14:28), that righteousness lifts a nation (14:34), and that God, the Maker of the poor, takes their oppression as an insult to himself (14:31). For a young official the sayings were both career advice and a check on power.
settings.readers: After the monarchy ended, Jews read these sayings about kings as wisdom for any ruler, including the foreign kings they lived under, and the church read them as a word to Christian rulers.
views: Many scholars think 14:28–35 and 16:10–15 come from a court setting.
Others think any Israelite needed sayings about kings, since everyone lived under one.

title: A Soft-Spoken Answer
sum: Chapter 15 begins with one of the most quoted sayings in the book: "A soft-spoken answer turns fury back, but a hurtful word makes anger climb" (15:1). It returns again and again to the tongue (15:1–2, 4, 7, 23, 28) and to the LORD, who sees everywhere (15:3), weighs sacrifice and prayer (15:8, 29), sees into Sheol itself (15:11) and defends the widow's boundary (15:25). Two "better" sayings, "A little, along with the fear of the LORD, is better than a big store of treasure" and "A plate of vegetables with love at the table is better than a stall-fed ox served with hatred" (15:16–17), closely match an Egyptian teaching.

The chapter ends the first half of the Solomon collection. 15:20 repeats the opening line of 10:1, and the last verse brings back the book's motto: "The fear of the LORD is wisdom's discipline, and before honor goes humility" (15:33). The sayings about the LORD that follow in 16:1–9 continue the theme.

views.H: The sayings on sacrifice and prayer (15:8, 29) assume the temple and its offerings, and the widow's boundary (15:25) the land system of Israel's villages, where a family's fields were marked by stones.
views.C: The Greek arranges the end of chapter 15 and the start of 16 differently, placing sayings from 16:6–9 among 15:27–29 and leaving out 15:31 (see below). Many scholars see 15:20 as an editor's frame with 10:1, or 15:33–16:9 as a seam between the two halves of the collection.
views.W: Amenemope's "Better is poverty in the hand of the god than riches in the storehouse" stands close to 15:16–17, and his warning against moving "the boundaries of a widow" to 15:25. Since 22:17–24:22 clearly knows Amenemope, these parallels may come from the same tradition.
views.J: The Mishnah's "an eye that sees, an ear that hears" (Mishnah Avot 2:1) echoes 15:3, and the Damascus Document quotes 15:8 to set the prayer of the righteous beside acceptable sacrifice.
views.X: Christian traditions have used 15:8 in a debate about whether the good works and worship of people without faith please God (see below). 15:1 is a staple of Christian teaching on peacemaking, and 15:33's humility before honor is echoed in Jesus' sayings (Luke 14:11).

deep.b: Chapter 15 names the LORD nine times, more than any chapter so far in the collection. He sees everywhere (15:3), even Sheol and Abaddon and the human heart (15:11). He judges worship by the worshiper: the sacrifice of the wicked is abhorrent and the prayer of the upright pleases him (15:8), and he is far from the wicked but hears the righteous (15:29). He pulls down the proud and defends the widow (15:25). A little with his fear is better than great wealth (15:16), and his fear is "wisdom's discipline" (15:33). The sages' practical advice about speech and money is set inside this picture of a God who watches, weighs and protects.

deep.h: The Greek order at the end of chapter 15
deep.b: In Codex Vaticanus, as Swete prints it, the end of chapter 15 also holds sayings that the Hebrew has in chapter 16: after 15:27 comes 16:6 (in the Greek, "By alms and faithful deeds sins are cleansed away"), after 15:28 comes 16:7, and after 15:29 come 16:8 and 16:9. Then follow 15:30, 15:32 and 15:33; there is no Greek for 15:31. Scholars explain the Greek arrangement as the translator's or as a different Hebrew order; Johann Cook argues that the translator often reshaped the book with a theological purpose. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew order.

traditions.q: Are the worship and good deeds of people without saving faith pleasing to God, or are they sin in his sight?
views: Not all works done before justification are sins. Trent condemned the view that every work done before justification is truly sin, and taught that grace prompts and helps people toward justification even before they are justified (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapters 5–6 and canon 7).

Human beings can achieve a civil righteousness by reason, and it has real worth in this world, but without faith no work can please God or merit grace (Augsburg Confession, articles 18 and 20; Apology, article 4).

Works done by those not born again may be good in what is done, yet they are sinful before God, because they do not come from a heart purified by faith or aim at God's glory (Westminster Confession 16.7). Verses such as 15:8 are read in this light.
Works done before the grace of Christ and the inspiration of his Spirit are not pleasing to God, and "have the nature of sin" (Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 13).

God's prevenient grace is at work in every person before conversion, so the good that people do is already a response to grace, though it does not justify them (Wesley, sermon "On Working Out Our Own Salvation").

echoes: Judges 8:1–3; 1 Samuel 25:23–35; 1 Kings 12:13–16; 2 Chronicles 16:9; 1 Samuel 15:22; Isaiah 1:11–17; Amos 5:21–24; Job 26:6; Revelation 9:11; Deuteronomy 19:14; Deuteronomy 27:17; Exodus 23:8; Psalm 34:15; Luke 14:11; 10:1; 16:1–9

settings.what: Sayings on gentle speech, the LORD who sees, better a little, and humility
settings.by: the sages of the first Solomon collection
settings.to: young men learning to speak, to worship and to handle wealth, and through them their households
settings.when: in the same collection, at the end of its first half (10:1–15:33)
settings.why: To teach self-control in speech (15:1–2, 23, 28), honest worship (15:8, 29), contentment with little (15:16–17) and humility (15:33), all under the eyes of a God who sees every place and heart (15:3, 11). Knowing that these were sayings for the young explains the stress on listening and accepting rebuke (15:5, 10, 12, 31–32).
settings.readers: For Jews after the exile, when the temple was rebuilt but often poorly led, 15:8 and 15:29 echoed the prophets' call for worship joined to justice. Christian readers have found in 15:1 and 15:33 the spirit of the Sermon on the Mount.
views: Many scholars (for example McKane and Fox) think sayings like these were collected and used to train young scribes and officials at the court in Jerusalem, as Egyptian instructions were used in Egypt; 25:1 shows royal scribes at work on Proverbs.
Others (for example Claus Westermann) think most of the two-line sayings began as folk wisdom among farmers and households and were only later written down by scribes.
Most critical scholars think the collection reached its final form, with chapters 1–9 in front of it, in the Persian period, when the book became a textbook for Jewish life.
